note: Used until about 10-11 in the morning. The 'd' in 'god' is silent, so it sounds like 'goo morn'. Many Norwegians just say 'morn' or 'morn, morn'.

example.target: God morgen! Har du sovet godt?
example.en: Good morning! Did you sleep well?

note: The polite daytime greeting, now mostly heard in shops, offices and from older speakers. In casual talk 'hei' has largely replaced it.
'Kveld' is the Old Norse word for evening (kveld). Said on arriving in the evening, not when leaving.
Only for going to bed or parting late at night. 'Natt' is cognate with English 'night'; the plural is 'netter'.
The 'h' in 'hvordan' is silent (say 'vordan'). A real question, but the expected answer is short: 'Bare bra' or 'Det går bra'. Also 'Hvordan har du det?'
The standard reply to 'Hvordan går det?'. 'Bare' means 'only/just' and softens it: just fine, nothing special. Often followed by 'og med deg?' (and with you?).
Built like English 'welcome': 'vel' (well) + 'kommen' (come). 'Velkommen til Norge!' Same word for one or many people.
Warmer than plain 'takk'. 'Mange takk' (many thanks) also exists but is a bit old-fashioned.
Said when you meet someone again after a previous get-together, thanking them for last time. There is no English equivalent, and forgetting it can seem cold.

example.target: Hei, takk for sist! Det var en hyggelig kveld.
example.en: Hi, thanks for last time! It was a nice evening.

note: Said when handing something over, inviting someone to sit or eat, and as a reply to 'takk'. Often written 'værsågod' and pronounced as one word.

example.target: Vær så god, her er kaffen din.
example.en: Here you are, here is your coffee.

note: A relaxed reply to thanks: there is no reason to thank me. 'Bare hyggelig' (just a pleasure) is a friendlier alternative.
Literally 'I regret'. Used for apologies and bad news ('Beklager, vi er stengt'). For bumping into someone 'unnskyld' is more usual.
'Hyggelig' comes from 'hygge' (cosiness, good company), the same word Danish exported to English. 'Hyggelig å hilse på deg' is a common variant.
Pronounced 'ya'. Norwegians often say it while breathing in, a quick 'ja' on an inhale that means 'yes, I'm listening'.
Pronounced 'nye'. 'Nei takk' is 'no thanks'. Doubled and drawn out, 'nei nei', it means 'oh dear' rather than a strong refusal.
Answers a negative question or statement: 'Kommer du ikke?' – 'Jo!' (Yes, I am). English lost this distinction; Norwegian, French (si) and German (doch) keep it.

example.target: Liker du ikke fisk? – Jo, det gjør jeg.
example.en: Don't you like fish? – Yes, I do.

en: Say hello to everyone at home
note: 'Hils' is the imperative of 'å hilse' (to greet). 'Hils X fra meg' = say hi to X from me. The 'h' in 'hjemme' is silent.
The -s ending on 'ses' makes the verb reciprocal ('see each other'). Also 'Vi snakkes' (we'll talk) and 'Vi høres' (we'll be in touch).
Common from shop staff. 'Ha en fin helg' (have a nice weekend) is the Friday version. 'Fin' means fine, nice, pretty.
'Lykke' (luck, happiness) is a Low German loan from the Hanseatic period, related to German 'Glück'. The 'til' is left hanging: luck to (you).
The present tense of 'å gratulere', used on its own. Takes 'med' (with): 'Gratulerer med ny jobb!'
Norwegian has no separate 'happy birthday'; you congratulate someone 'with the day'. Also used on 17 May, the national day.
From Old Norse 'skál', a drinking bowl; English borrowed it as 'skoal'. Make eye contact, say skål, drink, then eye contact again.
'Tur' covers everything from a walk in the woods to a flight abroad. Said to anyone setting off, including hikers heading out the door.
A warm, slightly emphatic thank-you, often said when receiving something or help. Word-for-word 'thanks shall you have'.
From Latin 'nullus' (none), like German 'Null'. Pronounced with a short 'u' as in 'pull'.
Agrees with the noun's gender: 'én bil', 'ei/en jente', 'ett hus'. The accent on 'én' just marks stress to distinguish it from the article 'en' (a).
Cognate with English 'two' and Old Norse 'tveir'. The old gender forms (tvo, tvei) are gone; 'to' works for all genders.
Also the word for 'tree' and 'wood' (et tre). Context makes it clear: 'tre trær' is three trees.
Looks like English 'fire' but is pronounced 'FEE-reh'. Cognate with English 'four'.
Short and regular. 'Femti' (fifty) and 'femten' (fifteen) are built on it.
Pronounced like English 'sex', which Norwegians find as funny as you do. Cognate with 'six'.
Both 'sju' and the older 'syv' are correct Bokmål; 'syv' is still common in Oslo and the east. Seventeen (sytten) and seventy (sytti) are built on 'syv'.
The letter 'å' sounds like 'aw' in 'law'. Cognate with English 'eight' and German 'acht'.
Pronounced 'nee'. Nineteen is 'nitten', ninety 'nitti'.
Pronounced 'tee'. Not to be confused with 'te' (tea), which has a more open 'e'.
Pronounced roughly 'EL-veh'; the middle 'e' is usually swallowed. Cognate with English 'eleven' (originally 'one left over' after ten).
The 'v' is silent: say 'toll'. Related to English 'twelve' ('two left over').
From 13 to 19 the pattern is unit + '-ten'. Note the double 't' and the spelling 'tre-' rather than 'tre'.
Not 'fireten': the old form 'fjor-' survives here, as in 'førti' (forty). 'Fjorten dager' (fourteen days) is the usual way to say a fortnight.
Regular: 'fem' + 'ten'. Stress on the first syllable.
Spelled 'seks' + 'ten' but pronounced 'SICE-ten' (the 'ks' becomes an 'ai' sound). One of the few irregular pronunciations among the numbers.
Built on the old form 'syv', not 'sju'. Pronounced 'SUT-ten' with the rounded Norwegian 'y'. 17 May (syttende mai) is Constitution Day.

example.en: The seventeenth of May is the national day.

note: The 'å' of 'åtte' becomes a plain 'a' here. The age of majority in Norway, so 'Er du atten?' is a common question at the bar.
Regular: 'ni' + 'ten' with a double 't'. Years are read in hundreds: 1990 = 'nitten nitti'.
'Tjue' (pronounced 'CHOO-eh') and the older 'tyve' are both correct. 21 is 'tjueen' in the new counting system or 'enogtyve' (one-and-twenty) in the old, which many older speakers still use.
The older form 'tredve' is still heard. Tens from 30 to 90 end in '-ti': tretti, førti, femti, seksti, sytti, åtti, nitti.
51 shows the two counting systems: 'femtién' (fifty-one, official since 1951, used on radio and in banks) and 'énogfemti' (one-and-fifty, the old way, still common in speech).
Usually without 'one': 'hundre kroner' = a hundred kroner. 'Ett hundre' is used only for emphasis. Cognate with English 'hundred'.
As in 'tusen takk'. Norwegian uses a space or dot as the thousands separator and a comma for decimals: 1 000,50.
Ordinals: første, andre (second), tredje, fjerde, femte, sjette, sjuende, åttende, niende, tiende. In dates a dot marks the ordinal: '1. mai' is read 'første mai'.

example.target: Dette er første gang jeg er i Norge.
example.en: This is the first time I am in Norway.

note: Definite form 'familien'. The 'ie' ending is pronounced 'ee-eh', with stress on the second syllable (fa-MEE-lee-eh).
Feminine: 'mora' or 'moren' in the definite form (Bokmål lets you use masculine 'en/-en' for any feminine noun). Plural is irregular: 'mødre'. Children say 'mamma'.
Definite 'faren', irregular plural 'fedre'. Children say 'pappa'. From Old Norse 'faðir', cognate with English 'father'.
Plural only; definite 'foreldrene'. For one parent you say 'en forelder' or more naturally 'mor eller far'.
Definite 'broren', irregular plural 'brødre'. Cognate with English 'brother'.
Definite 'søstera' or 'søsteren', plural 'søstre'. 'Søsken' is the plural word for siblings of either sex.

example.target: Jeg har to søstre og en bror.
example.en: I have two sisters and a brother.

note: Definite 'sønnen', plural 'sønner'. The '-sen' in surnames like Hansen and Olsen is the same word: Hans's son.
Definite 'dattera' or 'datteren', irregular plural 'døtre'. The 'dotter/-datter' surnames (e.g. Olsdatter) were used for women until the 1800s.
Neuter: 'barnet' (the child). The plural is the same as the singular, 'barn', so 'tre barn' is three children; definite plural 'barna'. Scottish 'bairn' is the same word.
'Beste' + 'mor'. Norwegians also specify which side: 'mormor' (mother's mother) and 'farmor' (father's mother).
Likewise 'morfar' (mother's father) and 'farfar' (father's father). Grandchild is 'barnebarn' (child's child).
From French 'oncle' via German, like English 'uncle'. Older native words survive in some dialects: 'morbror' (mother's brother) and 'farbror'.
A loan via German/French, like English 'aunt'. 'Tante' is also what small children sometimes call any friendly adult woman.
Definite 'mannen', irregular plural 'menn'. Also means husband: 'mannen min' = my husband. Feminine counterpart 'kvinne'; wife is 'kone'.
Definite 'kvinna/kvinnen', plural 'kvinner'. Cognate with English 'queen', which narrowed from 'woman' to 'king's wife'. For 'wife' use 'kone'.
Definite 'kona' or 'konen'. 'Kona mi' = my wife. Husband is simply 'mann' (mannen min), or formally 'ektemann'.
Definite 'gutten', plural 'gutter'. Also used for grown men among friends ('gutta' = the lads).
The classic feminine noun: 'ei jente, jenta'. Bokmål also allows 'en jente, jenten', but 'jenta' is what most people say. Plural 'jenter'.
Borrowed from English, pronounced the English way; definite 'babyen'. 'Et spedbarn' is the more formal word.
The superlative of 'kjær' (dear): your 'dearest'. Gender-neutral, so 'kjæresten min' can be a boyfriend or girlfriend. 'Kj' sounds like the 'h' in 'huge'.
Definite 'naboen'. From Old Norse 'nábúi' (near-dweller), the same idea as English 'neigh-bour' (near farmer).
'Folk' is used like English 'people' in general statements: 'Folk er hyggelige her'. It is also the root of 'folkemusikk' (folk music) and 'folkehøgskole' (folk high school).
Originally the past participle of 'å vokse' (to grow), so 'en voksen' is 'a grown one'. Plural 'voksne'. Also an adjective: 'voksne barn' (grown-up children).
Queen is 'dronning'. The royal palace in Oslo is 'Slottet'; the king is 'Kongen', and 'Kongehuset' is the royal family.
Your parent's sibling's child. More specific: 'fetter' (male cousin) and 'kusine' (female cousin), both loans via German/French.
Definite 'brødet'; 'ø' is like the vowel in 'bird'. Norwegians eat a lot of 'grovbrød' (coarse wholegrain bread) with 'pålegg' (toppings) for breakfast and lunch.
Definite 'melka' or 'melken'. 'Lettmelk' is semi-skimmed, 'helmelk' whole milk. Nynorsk has 'mjølk', closer to the Old Norse.

example.target: Kan jeg få melk i kaffen?
example.en: Can I have milk in the coffee?

note: Definite 'osten'. 'Ostehøvel', the cheese slicer, was invented in Norway in 1925 and is in every kitchen.
Sweet, caramel-coloured whey cheese, a national favourite on bread and waffles. 'Brun' (brown) + 'ost'. 'Geitost' is the goat's milk version.

example.target: Jeg vil ha vaffel med brunost.
example.en: I want a waffle with brown cheese.

note: Neuter: 'smøret'. The verb 'å smøre' means to spread/butter, and 'smørbrød' (butter-bread) is an open sandwich.
English 'egg' was borrowed from Old Norse 'egg', replacing native 'ey'. Neuter: 'egget'; plural 'egg', 'eggene'.
Neuter: 'kjøttet'. 'Kj' is a soft 'h' sound (as in 'huge'), though many young speakers now say it like 'sh'. 'Kjøttkaker' are Norwegian meatballs.
Definite 'fisken', plural 'fisk'. 'Fiskekaker' (fish cakes) and 'fiskesuppe' are everyday dishes; 'tørrfisk' (dried cod) was Norway's great medieval export.

example.en: We are having fish for dinner.

note: Definite 'laksen'. Norway is the world's biggest farmed salmon producer; 'røkelaks' is smoked salmon, 'gravlaks' is cured ('buried') salmon.
Definite 'pølsa'. 'Pølse i brød' (sausage in bread) or 'pølse i lompe' (in a potato flatbread) is the classic cheap meal from kiosks and petrol stations.
Definite 'poteten', plural 'poteter'. Boiled potatoes come with nearly every traditional dinner; 'potetgull' (potato gold) is crisps.
'Grønn' (green) + 'sak' (thing, matter). Usually plural: 'grønnsaker'.
Neuter: 'eplet', plural 'epler'. Hardanger in western Norway is famous for apple orchards and 'eplesaft' (apple juice).
'Jord' (earth, soil) + 'bær' (berry). Norwegian summer strawberries, ripened slowly in the long days, are a seasonal obsession. The 'd' in 'jord' is silent.
Definite 'kaka' or 'kaken'. English 'cake' is itself a loan from Old Norse 'kaka'. 'Bløtkake' is the cream-layer cake served on 17 May.
Neuter: 'sukkeret'. Pronounced 'SOOK-ker'. 'Sukkerfri' means sugar-free.
Neuter: 'vannet'. Also means a lake, so many lakes are called '-vann'. Nynorsk has 'vatn', closer to English 'water'. Tap water is drunk everywhere.
Neuter: 'ølet'; 'en øl' means one (glass of) beer. From Old Norse 'ǫl', cognate with English 'ale'. Alcohol is heavily taxed, so beer is expensive.
Definite 'vinen'. Wine and spirits are sold only at the state monopoly, Vinmonopolet, nicknamed 'Polet'. 'Rødvin' red, 'hvitvin' white.
'Mat' (food) + 'pakke' (package). The slices of bread with pålegg wrapped in paper that most Norwegians take to school or work instead of buying lunch.

example.target: Har du med matpakke i dag?
example.en: Have you brought a packed lunch today?

note: From Low German 'vrōkost' (early meal), a Hanseatic loan. Beware: in Danish 'frokost' means lunch.
Borrowed from English and respelled: 'sj' is the Norwegian 'sh'. Often eaten early, around 11-12, and often just a matpakke.
Literally 'midday', because the main meal was once eaten then. Today 'middag' is the hot meal of the day, often as early as 4-5 pm.

example.target: Hva skal vi ha til middag?
example.en: What shall we have for dinner?

note: A regular verb (past '-te'). Low German loan 'spisen'; the older native 'å ete' is now mostly used for animals or in Nynorsk.

example.en: We eat dinner at five o'clock.

note: A strong verb: drikker, drakk, har drukket, like English drink/drank/drunk. 'Drikke' is also a noun for a drink.
Definite 'kafeen'. The accent marks the stress on the last syllable. Spelled 'kafé' in Norwegian, although 'kaffe' (the drink) has double f and no accent.
French loan; pronounced roughly 'resto-RANG' with a nasal ending. Definite 'restauranten'.
Definite 'menyen'. The 'y' is the rounded vowel, like French 'u'. 'Dagens' (today's) is the daily special.
Definite 'koppen'. 'En kopp kaffe' = a cup of coffee, with no word for 'of'. Norway has one of the world's highest coffee consumptions per person.
Neuter: 'glasset'. Note the double 's'; 'glass' is also the material. 'Et glass vin' = a glass of wine.
Definite 'flaska' or 'flasken'. Bottles carry a deposit ('pant'); returning them to the shop machine is 'å pante'.
Neuter: 'bordet'. The 'd' is silent: 'boor'. Cognate with English 'board', as in 'room and board'.
'Til' (to, for) is the preposition for 'for' here. 'Har dere et bord til to?' = Do you have a table for two?

example.target: Har dere et bord til to?
example.en: Do you have a table for two?

note: From French 'serviteur'. The feminine 'servitrise' exists but 'servitør' is now used for everyone. Call them with 'unnskyld', not by snapping fingers.
From 'en regning' (bill, invoice; from 'å regne', to calculate). 'Kan jeg få regningen?' You usually pay at the table by card; splitting is normal.

example.en: Can we have the bill, please?

note: Low German loan ('bestellen'). Also means to book: 'å bestille bord' (to book a table), 'å bestille time' (to make an appointment).
The everyday way to order: 'Kan jeg få en kaffe?' 'Få' (to get) is used where English says 'have'. Add 'takk' at the end rather than 'vær så snill'.

example.target: Kan jeg få en kopp te?
example.en: Can I have a cup of tea?

note: 'Gjerne' (gladly) softens 'vil ha' (want). The 'g' in 'gjerne' is silent: 'YER-neh'. A polite, slightly fuller way to order than 'Kan jeg få'.
Definite 'bollen'. Soft cardamom buns, often with raisins; 'skolebolle' has custard and coconut. Also means 'bowl', so 'bolle' is both the bun and what you mix it in.
Definite 'vaffelen', plural 'vafler'. Norwegian waffles are heart-shaped and soft, eaten with jam, sour cream or brunost.

en: Enjoy your meal / you're welcome (after a meal)
note: From German 'wohl bekomm's'. Said when serving food, and as the host's reply to 'takk for maten'.
'For-' (before) + 'rett' (dish, course). 'Rett' also means 'right/correct' and 'straight'.
'Hoved' (head, main) + 'rett' (dish). The 'd' in 'hoved' is silent.
French loan, pronounced 'des-SÆR' with the final 't' silent, as in French. Definite 'desserten'.
Borrowed from English. Tipping is optional in Norway because staff earn a living wage; rounding up or 5-10% for good service is appreciated but not expected.
Definite 'gaffelen', plural 'gafler'. From Low German 'gaffel' (fork); the same word is used for a ship's gaff.
Definite 'kniven'. The 'k' is pronounced, unlike in English 'knife', which was borrowed from Old Norse 'knífr'.
Definite 'skjea' or 'skjeen'. 'Skj' is pronounced 'sh': 'shay'. 'En teskje' is a teaspoon.
Definite 'tallerkenen'. A Low German loan ('tallorken'), ultimately from Italian 'tagliere' (cutting board).
Both 'to taste something' and 'to taste of': 'Det smaker godt' (it tastes good). 'Smak' is the noun, as in 'god smak' (good taste).
Definite 'reisa' or 'reisen'. From Low German 'reise', a Hanseatic loan (German 'Reise'). 'God reise!' = have a good journey.
Regular verb with '-te' past. 'Å reise bort' = to go away. Also 'to raise', as in 'å reise seg' (to stand up).

example.target: Vi reiser til Bergen i morgen.
example.en: We are travelling to Bergen tomorrow.

note: From Latin 'feriae' (festival days) via German 'Ferien'. 'Fellesferie', the common July holiday, is when much of Norway shuts down.

example.en: I am on holiday in July.

note: Neuter: 'passet'. Short for 'passport', as in English. Also means a mountain pass and 'to fit' (å passe).
From French 'billet'; stress on the last syllable. Definite 'billetten'. 'Enkeltbillett' is a single, 'tur-retur' a return.
Neuter: 'kartet'. From French 'carte'; the same word as English 'chart'. Not 'mappe', which means a folder.
'Venstre' is also the name of a political party (the Liberals), founded in 1884 as the 'left'. 'På venstre side' = on the left-hand side.
'Høyre' is also the Conservative party. The 'øy' diphthong sounds like 'uh-ee'. 'Rett' (not 'høyre') is the word for 'right' as in 'correct'.
'Rett' = straight/right/correct. 'Fram' and 'frem' are both allowed spellings; Nynorsk uses 'fram'.

example.target: Gå rett fram, så ser du stasjonen.
example.en: Go straight ahead and you will see the station.

note: Silent 'h': 'voor ær'. 'Hvor er toalettet?' is the one to learn first. Nynorsk has 'kor' instead of 'hvor'.

example.en: Excuse me, where is the toilet?

note: The neuter form of 'lang' (long), used adverbially: 'Er det langt?' (Is it far?). 'Langt unna' = far away.
'Nær stasjonen' = near the station. Cognate with English 'near'. 'I nærheten' = nearby, in the vicinity.
Pronounced 'hær'. 'Hit' means 'to here' (motion): 'Kom hit!' = come here, but 'Jeg bor her' = I live here.
Pronounced 'dær'. As with 'her/hit', motion uses a different form: 'dit' (to there). 'Der borte' = over there.
Definite 'gata' (the usual form) or 'gaten'. From Old Norse 'gata'; English 'gate' in northern street names like Briggate comes from the same word.
Neuter: 'hjørnet'. The 'h' is silent: 'YUR-neh'. 'Rundt hjørnet' = around the corner.
Definite 'veien'. Street signs end in '-veien' (Kirkeveien). Also 'way' in the abstract: 'på vei' = on the way, 'Vis meg veien' = show me the way. Nynorsk: 'veg'.

example.en: Is this the way to the centre?

note: The 'd' is silent: 'noor'. 'Nord-Norge' is Northern Norway. The adverb 'nordover' = northwards.
'Sørlandet' (the south country) is Norway's southern coast. 'Syd' is an older, Danish-flavoured form still seen in names.
'Østlandet' is the eastern region around Oslo. Cognate with English 'east'.
'Vestlandet' is the fjord country around Bergen. Also means a waistcoat (en vest).
'Fly' (aeroplane) + 'plass' (place, square). Definite 'flyplassen'. Oslo's airport is Gardermoen; 'lufthavn' (air harbour) is the official word.

example.en: How do I get to the airport?

note: Strong verb: finner, fant, har funnet. 'Å finne fram' = to find your way. Cognate with English 'find'.
Definite 'turen'. 'Å gå på tur' (to go for a walk/hike) is a national pastime; 'tur' covers a stroll, a hike, a drive or a journey.

example.target: Skal vi gå på tur i helgen?
example.en: Shall we go for a hike at the weekend?

note: Neuter: 'hotellet'. Stress on the last syllable, as in French. Note the double 'l' in Norwegian spelling.
Definite 'bilen', plural 'biler'. Clipped from 'automobil' around 1900; Danish and Swedish use the same word. Norway has the world's highest share of electric cars ('elbil').

example.en: The car is parked outside the house.

note: Neuter: 'toget'. Pronounced 'tawg'. The same word means a parade ('17. mai-tog'). Trains are run by Vy and others on the national network.
Definite 'bussen'. Double 's' in Norwegian spelling. 'Å ta bussen' = to take the bus.
Neuter: 'flyet', plural 'fly'. Literally 'a fly(ing thing)'; the verb is also 'å fly'. Domestic flights are common because of the long distances.
Definite 'båten'. Cognate with English 'boat'. Many families own a small boat; 'hurtigbåt' is a fast passenger ferry.
Definite 'ferja'. From Old Norse 'ferja'; English 'ferry' is related. Car ferries across the fjords are part of the road network on the west coast.

example.en: We take the ferry across the fjord.

note: Definite 'sykkelen', plural 'sykler'. From 'bicycle' with the 'bi-' dropped. 'Y' is a rounded vowel, like French 'u'.
Definite 'trikken'. Clipped from 'elektrisk' (electric) when electric trams replaced horse trams in Oslo in the 1890s. Oslo, Bergen and Trondheim have trams.
Short for 'tunnelbane'. Only Oslo has one; the blue 'T' sign marks stations. 'Bane' means track or railway.

example.en: I take the metro to work.

note: From Russian 'drozhki' (a light carriage) via German 'Droschke'. 'Taxi' is equally common; taxis are expensive in Norway.
Definite 'stasjonen'. The 'sj' spelling shows the 'sh' sound; stress on the last syllable. 'Jernbanestasjon' = railway station.
'Holde' (to hold, stop) + 'plass' (place). 'Bussholdeplass' in full. Press 'stopp' to get off.
Regular verb. 'Kj' is a soft 'h' sound: 'HYUR-eh'. Also used for riding in a vehicle: 'å kjøre buss' = to go by bus.

example.target: Kan du kjøre meg til stasjonen?
example.en: Can you drive me to the station?

note: Strong verb: flyr, fløy, har fløyet. Cognate with English 'fly'. The noun 'et fly' is a plane.
Regular verb formed from 'sykkel'; note the single 'k' in the verb. 'Å sykle til jobb' = to cycle to work.
Norwegian uses the definite form here ('the bus') where English can say 'take a bus'. Same pattern: 'ta toget', 'ta trikken', 'ta fly' (plane, no article).

example.en: I take the bus every day.

note: Definite 'bensinen'. From German 'Benzin'. 'Bensinstasjon' is a petrol station, which in Norway also sells hot dogs and coffee.
'Fører' (driver, leader) + 'kort' (card). Neuter: 'førerkortet'. Also called 'lappen' (the slip): 'å ta lappen' = to get your licence.
'Motor' + 'vei'. Few and short by European standards; the general speed limit is 80 km/h, 110 on motorways.
'Parkering' + joining '-s-' + 'plass'. The '-s-' is a common glue between parts of a compound. 'Parkering forbudt' = no parking.
'Bru' and 'bro' are both correct Bokmål; 'bru' is closer to Old Norse 'brú'. Definite 'brua'. Cognate with English 'bridge'.
Definite 'tunnelen'. Norway has over a thousand road tunnels, including Lærdalstunnelen, the world's longest at 24.5 km.
Regular verb. Both 'stop (yourself)' and 'stop something'. 'Stopp!' as a sign; 'neste stopp' = next stop.
'Av' (off) + 'gang' (going). Shown on boards as 'Avgang'. The verb is 'å gå' used of transport: 'Toget går klokka ti' = the train leaves at ten.
'An-' + 'komst' (coming), a Low German-style formation. Airport boards show 'Ankomst' and 'Avgang'.
Definite 'dagen', plural 'dager'. The 'g' is silent: 'daag'. 'Hele dagen' = all day. 'I dag' (today) is two words.
Definite 'natta' or 'natten', irregular plural 'netter'. 'I natt' means both 'last night' and 'tonight' (the coming night); context decides.
Definite 'uka' or 'uken', plural 'uker'. Norwegians refer to weeks by number: 'uke 8' is the winter holiday. Nynorsk: 'veke', closer to English 'week'.
Definite 'måneden', plural 'måneder'. The 'd' is silent. From 'måne' (moon), as English 'month' is from 'moon'.
Neuter: 'året'; plural same as singular: 'to år'. 'Godt nyttår!' = Happy New Year. Cognate with English 'year'.
Definite 'timen'. Pronounced 'TEE-meh', not like English 'time'. Also a lesson at school or an appointment: 'bestille time hos legen'.
Neuter: 'minuttet', plural 'minutter'. Stress on the last syllable. 'Vent et minutt' = wait a minute.
Two words in Norwegian ('idag' is a common misspelling). The same 'i' pattern gives 'i morgen', 'i går', 'i kveld' (tonight), 'i år' (this year).
Literally 'in the morning', but it means tomorrow. 'Tomorrow morning' is 'i morgen tidlig' (tomorrow early).
'Går' here is an old word for yesterday (Old Norse 'gær'), unrelated to the verb 'går' (goes). 'I forgårs' = the day before yesterday.
Pronounced 'naw'. 'Nå' can also open a sentence as a filler ('Nå, hva skal vi gjøre?'). Cognate with English 'now'.
Days of the week are lower-case in Norwegian. 'På mandag' = on Monday; 'om mandagen' or 'på mandager' = on Mondays.
Named after the Norse god Tyr, as English 'Tuesday' is after his Anglo-Saxon counterpart Tiw. The 'g' in '-dag' is silent in all the day names.
Odin's day, as 'Wednesday' is Woden's. Pronounced 'ONS-daag'.
Thor's day. Thor is still a common first name, and 'torden' is thunder.
Named after the goddess Frigg (or Freya). 'Fredagstaco' (Friday tacos) has become a national family tradition.
From Old Norse 'laugardagr', bath day, when the Vikings washed. Unlike English, no planet in the name. 'Lørdagsgodt' is the Saturday sweets children get.
From Old Norse 'sunnudagr', the sun's day, like English 'Sunday'. Most shops are closed on Sundays by law; it is a day for 'søndagstur', the Sunday walk.
From Old Norse 'helgr', a holy day, related to 'hellig' (holy). Definite 'helga' or 'helgen'. 'God helg!' = have a good weekend. 'Weekend' is also used.

example.target: Hva skal du gjøre i helga?
example.en: What are you doing at the weekend?

note: Norwegian asks what 'the clock' is. Answer: 'Klokka er tre' (it is three). 'Klokka' is the feminine definite of 'klokke' (clock, bell); 'klokken' is also correct.

example.en: Excuse me, what time is it?

note: Warning: 'halv tre' means half TO three, i.e. 2:30, not 3:30. Norwegian looks ahead to the coming hour, like German 'halb drei'. The 'v' is silent.

example.en: We meet at half past seven.

note: From 'tid' (time). The 'd' and final 'g' are both silent: 'TEE-li'. 'For tidlig' = too early.
The adverb form of 'sen' (late). 'For sent' = too late; 'å komme for sent' = to be late. Not related to English 'sent'.

example.target: Jeg kom for sent til toget.
example.en: I was late for the train.

note: Months are lower-case and mostly Latin-based: januar, februar, mars, april, mai, juni, juli, august, september, oktober, november, desember. 'I januar' = in January.
Spelled with 's', not 'c', like 'sentrum' and 'sirkel'. Christmas is 'jul' (Yule), celebrated on the evening of 24 December, 'julaften'.
Adjectives agree: 'rød bil', 'rødt hus' (neuter), 'røde biler' (plural). The 'd' is silent. Classic red wooden houses are painted with 'rødmaling'.
Neuter 'blått', plural 'blå'. Cognate with English 'blue'. 'Blåbær' are bilberries, picked in the forests in August.
Neuter 'grønt', plural 'grønne'. From the same root as 'gro' (to grow), like English 'green/grow'.
Neuter 'gult', plural 'gule'. Cognate with English 'yellow' and 'gold'. Easter in Norway is yellow: 'påskegul'.
Neuter 'svart', plural 'svarte'. Cognate with English 'swarthy'. 'Sort' is an older Danish-style form still seen in print.
Silent 'h': 'veet'. Neuter 'hvitt', plural 'hvite'. Cognate with English 'white'. Nynorsk: 'kvit'.
Neuter 'grått', plural 'grå'. A 'gråvær' day is grey, overcast weather, a frequent topic in Bergen.
Neuter 'brunt', plural 'brune'. As in 'brunost'. 'Å bli brun' = to get a tan.
Does not change for gender or number: 'et rosa hus'. From Latin 'rosa' (rose). 'Lyserød' (light red) is an older alternative.
Invariable, like 'rosa'. From 'lilac'. 'Fiolett' is the more technical violet.
Invariable. Respelled from French 'orange' with 'sj' for the 'sh/zh' sound. The fruit is 'appelsin' (Low German 'apple from China').
Definite 'fargen', plural 'farger'. From Low German 'varwe', like German 'Farbe'. 'Hvilken farge?' = which colour?

example.en: Which colour do you like best?

note: Neuter 'mørkt', plural 'mørke'. 'Mørkeblå' = dark blue. 'Mørketida' (the dark time) is the sunless winter period in the north. Cognate with 'murky'.
'Lyseblå' = light blue. Also a noun: 'et lys' is a light or a candle, and 'lyse netter' are the bright summer nights.
Definite 'sirkelen', plural 'sirkler'. Spelled with 's' for the Latin 'c'. 'Polarsirkelen' is the Arctic Circle.
'Fir' (four) + 'kant' (edge). Covers rectangles too; 'kvadrat' is the precise square. 'Firkantet' = square, or figuratively rigid.
'Tre' (three) + 'kant' (edge). Same pattern as 'firkant'. 'Varseltrekant' is the warning triangle in your car.
Neuter 'rundt', plural 'runde'. 'Rundt' is also the preposition 'around': 'rundt hjørnet'. 'Rundkjøring' = roundabout.
Definite 'formen'. Also a baking tin ('kakeform') and fitness: 'i god form' = in good shape.
Definite 'stripa' or 'stripen'. 'Stripete' = striped. Related to English 'stripe'.
Definite 'prikken'. 'Prikkete' = spotted, polka-dot. 'Prikken over i-en' (the dot over the i) = the finishing touch.
Definite 'linja' or 'linjen'. Also a bus or metro line ('linje 5') and a study programme at upper secondary school.
Definite 'stjerna' or 'stjernen'. Pronounced 'STYÆR-neh'. Cognate with English 'star'. 'Stjerneklart' = starry (clear) sky.
Definite 'kanten'. The building block of 'firkant' and 'trekant'. Also a region: 'på disse kanter' = in these parts.
Definite 'kula'. A sphere, a marble or a bullet. As slang, 'kul' means 'cool' (from English), so 'kult!' = cool!
Neuter: 'hodet'. Body parts normally take the definite form instead of 'my': 'Jeg har vondt i hodet' = I have a headache (pain in the-head).
Neuter: 'ansiktet'. From Low German 'angesicht' (German 'Angesicht'). The Old Norse word survives in Nynorsk 'andlet'.
Neuter with an irregular plural: 'øyne', definite 'øynene'. Old Norse 'auga' gave the second half of 'vindauga', English 'window' (wind-eye).
Neuter: 'øret', plural 'ører'. Also the 1/100 of a krone (now only on paper). Cognate with English 'ear'.
Definite 'nesa' or 'nesen'. 'Nes' (headland, nose of land) is the same word, found in place names like Snarøya and Ness.
Definite 'munnen'. 'Munnbind' is a face mask. 'Å holde munn' = to keep quiet.
Irregular plural 'tenner', like English tooth/teeth. 'Tannlege' (tooth doctor) is the dentist; dental care for adults is not covered by the public system.
Definite 'halsen'. 'Vondt i halsen' = a sore throat. 'Nakke' is the back of the neck.
Definite 'armen', plural 'armer'. Same as English. 'Armbånd' (arm band) is a bracelet.
Irregular plural 'hender'. 'Hånd' and 'hand' are both accepted spellings. The 'd' is silent. 'Å håndhilse' = to shake hands.
Definite 'fingeren', plural 'fingre'. Pronounced with a hard 'g' as in 'finger', not 'singer'.
Neuter: 'beinet'. Means both leg and bone, like German 'Bein'. 'Ben' is an alternative spelling. Cognate with English 'bone'.
Irregular plural 'føtter', like foot/feet. 'Fotball' = football. 'Til fots' = on foot.
Definite 'magen'. 'Vondt i magen' = stomach ache. Pronounced 'MAA-geh'.
Neuter: 'hjertet'. Silent 'h': 'YÆR-teh'. Cognate with English 'heart'. 'Hjertelig' = hearty, heartfelt.
Definite 'ryggen'. Cognate with English 'ridge'; a mountain ridge is also 'en rygg'. 'Ryggsekk' = rucksack.
Neuter 'sykt', plural 'syke'. Cognate with English 'sick'. Nynorsk: 'sjuk'. 'Sykemelding' is a doctor's sick note.
Both 'healthy' (the opposite of 'syk') and 'fresh' (frisk luft = fresh air). 'God bedring!' = get well soon.
Definite 'legen'. From Old Norse 'læknir' (healer); English 'leech' (old word for doctor) is related. Everyone is assigned a 'fastlege' (GP).

example.target: Jeg må bestille time hos legen.
example.en: I have to make an appointment with the doctor.

note: 'Syke' (sick) + 'hus' (house). Neuter: 'sykehuset'. Emergency number 113; 'legevakt' is the out-of-hours clinic.
Neuter: 'apoteket'. From Greek 'apotheke' (storehouse) via Latin and German; 'apotekene' in the definite plural. Painkillers are also sold in supermarkets.
'Vondt' is the neuter of 'vond' (bad, painful). Pattern: 'ha vondt i' + body part in the definite: 'vondt i ryggen'. 'Det gjør vondt' = it hurts.
From 'kjøl' (cool), the idea of catching a chill. 'Å være forkjølet' = to have a cold. Not 'kald', which is only the temperature.
Definite 'feberen'. From Latin 'febris' via German. 'Å ha feber' = to have a temperature.
Definite 'medisinen'. Stress on the last syllable. Both the drug and the field of study. 'Resept' is a prescription.
Neuter: 'huset' (the house); plural 'hus', definite plural 'husene'. Most Norwegian houses are wooden and painted red, white or yellow.
Definite 'leiligheten', plural 'leiligheter'. From Low German 'legelicheit' (opportunity, convenience); 'leilighet' also still means 'occasion'.
Neuter: 'rommet', plural 'rom'. Also 'space' and 'Rome'. Cognate with English 'room'.
Definite 'stua' or 'stuen'. Old Norse 'stofa', originally the heated main room of a farmhouse. Cognate with English 'stove'.
Neuter: 'kjøkkenet'. From Low German 'kökene', ultimately Latin 'coquina', the same source as English 'kitchen'. 'Kj' is the soft 'h' sound.
'Sove' (sleep) + 'rom'. Neuter: 'soverommet'. Norwegians like to sleep with the window open even in winter.
Neuter: 'badet'. Means the bathroom and 'a bath/swim' ('å ta et bad'). The toilet is 'toalettet' or informally 'do'.
Definite 'døra' or 'døren', plural 'dører'. Cognate with English 'door'. 'Døra' is the usual spoken form.
From Old Norse 'vindauga' (wind + eye), the word the Vikings gave English as 'window'. Neuter: 'vinduet', plural 'vinduer'.
Neuter: 'gulvet'. Underfloor heating ('gulvvarme') is standard in Norwegian bathrooms. 'Golv' is an accepted alternative spelling.
Neuter: 'taket'. One word for both roof and ceiling. Not to be confused with 'takk' (thanks), which has a short vowel. Cognate with English 'thatch'.
Definite 'senga' or 'sengen', plural 'senger'. 'Å gå til sengs' or 'å legge seg' = to go to bed. 'Sengetøy' = bed linen.
Definite 'stolen'. Cognate with English 'stool', which narrowed in meaning while the Norwegian word kept 'chair'.
Definite 'sofaen'. Pronounced 'SOO-fa'. 'Sofakrok' is a cosy sofa corner, an important part of a koselig home.
'Kjøle' (to cool) + 'skap' (cupboard). Neuter: 'kjøleskapet'. The freezer is 'fryser' or 'fryseboks' (freeze box).

example.en: The milk is in the fridge.

note: Definite 'ovnen'. Pronounced 'ovn' with the 'v' audible. Also a heater: 'vedovn' is a wood-burning stove, common in cabins. 'Komfyr' is the cooker.
'Vaske' (wash) + 'maskin'. Compounds are written as one word in Norwegian; splitting them ('vaske maskin') is a famous spelling error called 'særskriving'.
Definite 'lampa' or 'lampen'. Norwegians love lamps and candles ('stearinlys') to counter the dark winters.
Definite 'nøkkelen', plural 'nøkler'. From Old Norse 'lykill'; the initial 'n' comes from the article 'en' sticking to it (en lykkel > en nykkel).
Silent 'h': 'YEM-meh'. Place: 'Jeg er hjemme' (I am at home). Motion uses 'hjem': 'Jeg går hjem' (I go home). Nynorsk: 'heime/heim'.
Definite 'hytta'. Related to German 'Hütte' and English 'hut'. Around half of Norwegians have access to a hytte in the mountains or by the sea; 'hyttetur' is a cabin trip.

example.target: Vi drar på hytta i påsken.
example.en: We are going to the cabin at Easter.

note: Definite 'hagen'. From Old Norse 'hagi' (enclosure, pasture); English 'hedge' and 'haw' are related. 'Barnehage' is a kindergarten.
Only for residing; 'to be alive' is 'å leve'. Regular: bor, bodde, har bodd. 'Hvor bor du?' = where do you live? Nynorsk: 'bu'.
Regular verb. 'Å rydde rommet' = to tidy the room; 'å rydde opp' = to clear up (also a mess or a problem). Nynorsk: 'rydde/rydja'.
Regular verb. 'Å vaske opp' = to wash up (dishes); 'å vaske seg' = to wash oneself. Cognate with English 'wash'.

example.target: Jeg må vaske opp etter middagen.
example.en: I have to wash up after dinner.

note: Plural only; definite 'klærne'. One item is 'et plagg'. 'Det finnes ikke dårlig vær, bare dårlige klær' (no bad weather, only bad clothes) is the national proverb.
Singular in Norwegian ('ei bukse', 'buksa'), unlike English 'trousers'. From Low German 'buxe', a contraction of 'bock-hose' (buckskin leggings).
Definite 'skjorta'. 'Skj' = 'sh'. From Old Norse 'skyrta', which also gave English 'skirt' (via Norse) and 'shirt' (native).
Definite 'genseren'. From English 'guernsey', the fisherman's sweater from the Channel Island. Norwegian patterned wool sweaters ('lusekofte', 'Marius-genser') are famous.

example.target: Ta på deg en genser, det er kaldt.
example.en: Put on a sweater, it is cold.

note: Definite 'jakka' or 'jakken'. 'Regnjakke' (rain jacket) and 'dunjakke' (down jacket) are the two essentials. Pronounced 'YAK-keh'.
Definite 'kjolen'. 'Kj' is the soft 'h' sound: 'HYOO-leh'. 'Brudekjole' = wedding dress.
Neuter: 'skjørtet'. Pronounced 'shurt'. A later borrowing of the same root as 'skjorte'; compare English shirt/skirt.
Definite 'skoen', plural 'sko', definite plural 'skoene'. Shoes come off at the door in every Norwegian home; expect to be in socks indoors.

example.target: Ta av deg skoene, er du snill.

note: Definite 'støvelen', plural 'støvler'. 'Gummistøvler' are wellies, 'vinterstøvler' insulated winter boots.
Definite 'lua'. The woolly hat worn from October to April. A hat with a brim is 'en hatt'; a cap is 'en caps'.
Definite 'votten', plural 'votter'. Mittens, warmer than gloves ('hansker'). 'Selbuvotter' with the eight-petal rose pattern are a Norwegian classic.
Neuter: 'skjerfet'. Pronounced 'shærf'. Borrowed from English 'scarf' and respelled with Norwegian 'skj'.
Definite 'sokken', plural 'sokker'. 'Ullsokker' (wool socks) are the indoor footwear of choice in winter.
English 'T-shirt' with 'skjorte' substituted for 'shirt'. Pronounced 'TEH-shor-teh'.
A false friend: 'en dress' is a man's suit, not a dress. A dress is 'en kjole'. From English 'dress' in the sense of outfit.
Definite 'ulla' or 'ullen'. 'Ull er gull' (wool is gold) is a national motto; children wear 'ullundertøy' (wool base layers) all winter. Cognate with English 'wool'.
'Under' + 'tøy' (cloth, stuff). Neuter: 'undertøyet'. 'Tøy' also means clothes informally ('vaske tøy' = do laundry).
Definite 'lomma' or 'lommen'. 'Lommebok' (pocket book) is a wallet; 'lommepenger' = pocket money; 'lommelykt' = torch.
Definite 'knappen'. The 'k' is pronounced. Also means 'scarce': 'knapp tid' = little time, 'knapt' = barely.
'Glide' (to glide, slide) + 'lås' (lock). A transparent compound, like German 'Reißverschluss' is not.
The usual way to say 'wear': 'Hun har på seg en rød kjole'. 'Seg' changes with the subject: 'jeg har på meg', 'du har på deg'.

example.target: Hva har du på deg i dag?

note: Reflexive: 'kle på seg' (get dressed), 'kle av seg' (get undressed). 'Å kle på barna' = to dress the children. 'Kle' is related to 'klær'.
'Ta av deg skoene' = take off your shoes. The opposite is 'å ta på seg' (to put on). The reflexive 'seg/meg/deg' is required.
Definite 'størrelsen'. From 'stor' (big) + '-else' (a noun ending, like English '-ness'). 'Hvilken størrelse bruker du?' = what size do you take?

example.target: Har dere denne i en større størrelse?
example.en: Do you have this in a bigger size?

note: Definite 'bunaden'. The regional folk costume worn on 17 May, weddings and confirmations; each district has its own pattern. Often inherited and very expensive.
Definite 'jobben'. From English 'job', with a double 'b' in Norwegian. 'På jobb' = at work. 'Jobb' is informal; 'arbeid' is the fuller word.

example.target: Jeg skal på jobb klokka åtte.
example.en: I am going to work at eight.

note: Regular verb formed from 'jobb'. The everyday verb; 'å arbeide' is more formal. 'Hvor jobber du?' = where do you work?
From Low German 'arbeiden' (German 'arbeiten'), a Hanseatic loan. The noun 'arbeid' is used in 'Arbeiderpartiet' (the Labour Party) and 'arbeidsledig' (unemployed).
Neuter: 'kontoret'. From French 'comptoir' (counter) via German 'Kontor', the name for a Hanseatic trading post such as the one in Bergen.
Definite 'sjefen'. From French 'chef' (chief); 'sj' = 'sh'. Norwegian workplaces are flat and first names are used for the boss too.
Definite 'kollegaen', plural 'kollegaer' or 'kolleger'. Stress on the second syllable: 'kol-LEH-ga'.
Definite 'læreren', plural 'lærere'. The feminine 'lærerinne' is dated and now avoided; 'lærer' is used for women too. Note that 'lærer' is also the present tense of 'å lære'.
Definite 'eleven'. From French 'élève'. Used for school pupils; university students are 'studenter'.
Definite 'studenten'. Stress on the last syllable. Public universities charge no tuition; 'Lånekassen' gives student loans.
Definite 'skolen'. Children start at six; 'barneskole', 'ungdomsskole' and 'videregående' are the three stages. Nynorsk: 'skule'.
Neuter: 'universitetet'. Stress on the final '-tet'. UiO (Oslo, 1811) is the oldest; NTNU in Trondheim is the largest.
Definite 'boka' or 'boken', irregular plural 'bøker'. From Old Norse 'bók', originally 'beech', since runes were cut into beechwood; English 'book' has the same story.
Definite 'pennen'. Double 'n'. 'Kulepenn' (ball pen) is a ballpoint, 'blyant' a pencil.
Neuter: 'papiret'. Stress on the last syllable. 'Papirer' (plural) = documents, as in English.
Also means 'to study' in the sense of revising: 'å lese til eksamen'. Regular: leser, leste, har lest.

example.en: I am reading a Norwegian book.

note: Strong verb: skriver, skrev, har skrevet. Ultimately from Latin 'scribere', like English 'scribe' and German 'schreiben'.
Means both: 'Jeg lærer norsk' (I am learning Norwegian) and 'Hun lærer meg norsk' (she teaches me). 'Å lære seg' makes it clearly 'learn'.

example.en: I am learning Norwegian at an evening class.

note: For studying a subject at university: 'Hun studerer medisin'. For doing homework or revising, use 'lese' or 'øve'. Stress on '-de-'.
Neuter: 'møtet'. From the verb 'å møte' (to meet). 'Jeg sitter i møte' = I am in a meeting.
Definite 'lønna' or 'lønnen'. Also 'reward'. 'Lønnsslipp' is a payslip. Salaries are public: tax records can be looked up online.
Definite 'leksa', usually plural 'lekser'. From Latin 'lectio' (a reading). 'Å gjøre lekser' = to do homework.
Neuter: 'faget', plural 'fag'. Also a trade or profession ('fagarbeider' = skilled worker). 'Fagforening' = trade union.
Definite 'pausen'. Pronounced 'POW-seh'. 'Lunsjpause' = lunch break; 'friminutt' is the break between lessons at school.
'Skue' (to view, show) + 'spiller' (player). The feminine 'skuespillerinne' (actress) still exists but 'skuespiller' is increasingly used for all.
'Data' + 'maskin'. Often shortened to 'data' or 'PC' (pronounced 'peh-seh'). 'Laptop' is also used.
Neuter: 'været'. The top topic of small talk. 'Hvordan er været?' = what is the weather like? Same spelling as the imperative 'vær' (be).
Definite 'sola' or 'solen'. 'Sola skinner' = the sun is shining. 'Midnattssol' is the midnight sun north of the Arctic Circle in summer.
Neuter: 'regnet'. The 'g' is silent: 'rayn'. Bergen gets rain on more than 200 days a year and sells umbrellas accordingly.
Impersonal with 'det': 'Det regner' (it is raining). Same spelling as 'å regne' = to calculate, from which 'regning' (bill) comes.

example.en: It is raining in Bergen again.

note: Definite 'snøen'. Cognate with English 'snow'. Snow vocabulary is rich: 'nysnø' (fresh), 'sludd' (sleet), 'skare' (crust), 'puddersnø' (powder).
Impersonal: 'Det snør'. Past 'snødde'. 'Det snør inn' = snow is drifting in.
Definite 'vinden'. The 'd' is silent: 'vinn'. 'Det blåser' = it is windy (literally 'it blows'). The first half of 'vindu' (window).
A false friend: 'sky' means cloud, not sky. English 'sky' was borrowed from Old Norse 'ský' (cloud) and shifted meaning. The sky is 'himmel'. Definite 'skya'.
Definite 'stormen'. On the Beaufort scale 'storm' is force 10, stronger than English usage; 'uvær' is bad weather generally.
Neuter 'kaldt', plural 'kalde'. 'Det er kaldt' = it is cold (neuter with 'det'). 'Jeg fryser' (I am freezing) is how you say you feel cold.

example.target: Det er kaldt ute i dag.

note: Neuter 'varmt', plural 'varme'. Covers both warm and hot; 'het' (hot) is rarer. 'Varmt vann' = hot water.
Definite 'vinteren', plural 'vintrer'. 'Om vinteren' = in (the) winter. Cognate with English 'winter'.
Definite 'våren'. 'Om våren' = in spring. Same spelling as the possessive 'vår' (our), so 'våren vår' = our spring.
Definite 'sommeren', plural 'somrer'. 'God sommer!' = have a good summer. Nynorsk: 'sommar'.
Definite 'høsten'. Literally 'harvest' (the verb 'å høste' = to harvest). Nynorsk: 'haust'. 'Høstferie' is the October school holiday.
Neuter: 'fjellet', plural 'fjell'. From Old Norse 'fjall'; English 'fell' (as in the Lake District) is the same word. 'Til fjells' = to the mountains.

example.target: Vi skal på fjellet i helga.
example.en: We are going to the mountains at the weekend.

note: Definite 'skogen'. From Old Norse 'skógr'; English 'shaw' (a thicket) is related. 'Skogstur' = a walk in the woods.
Definite 'elva'. The 'v' is pronounced. The Glomma is Norway's longest river. 'Bekk' is a stream.
Neuter: 'havet'. The 'v' is silent: 'haav'. 'Sjø' is also 'sea' (and 'lake' in some areas); 'til sjøs' = at sea.
Definite 'stranda'. The 'd' is silent. Cognate with English 'strand' (shore), as in the London street.
Neuter: 'treet', irregular plural 'trær'. Also means wood as a material and the number three. 'Juletre' = Christmas tree.
Definite 'blomsten', plural 'blomster'. Related to English 'bloom' and 'blossom'. Bringing flowers when invited to dinner is good manners.
Definite 'fjorden'. One of the few Norwegian words in English. The 'd' is silent: 'fyoor'. Related to 'ferd' (journey) and English 'ford'.
Definite 'øya'. The '-ey/-ay' in British island names like Orkney and Jersey is this Norse word. 'Øy' sounds like 'uh-ee'.
'Nord' (north) + 'lys' (light). Neuter: 'nordlyset'. Best seen in Tromsø and Finnmark from September to March.

example.target: Vi så nordlys i går kveld.
example.en: We saw the northern lights last night.

note: Definite 'butikken'. From French 'boutique'; stress on the last syllable. 'Matbutikk' = grocery shop. Most shops close early on Saturday and all day Sunday.
Plural only; definite 'pengene'. From Old Norse 'peningr', related to English 'penny'. 'Å tjene penger' = to earn money.
Definite 'prisen'. Also 'prize' and 'praise' ('Nobels fredspris'). From Low German/French 'pris'.
Silent 'h' in 'hva' and silent 't' in 'det': 'va KOS-ter deh'. 'Hva koster denne?' = how much is this one?

example.en: Excuse me, how much is this one?

note: Neuter 'billig', plural 'billige'. Final 'g' silent: 'BIL-li'. From Low German 'billik' (fair, reasonable). Rarely true in Norway.
Neuter 'dyrt', plural 'dyre'. Also 'dear' in the sense of beloved, like English 'dear'. 'Et dyr' with an article means 'an animal'.
Regular: kjøper, kjøpte, har kjøpt. From Old Norse 'kaupa'; English 'cheap' (originally 'trade') and the place-name element 'Chipping' share the same Germanic root.

example.target: Jeg kjøpte en ny jakke i går.
example.en: I bought a new jacket yesterday.

note: Irregular: selger, solgte, har solgt. The 'g' in 'solgt' is silent. 'Til salgs' = for sale. Cognate with English 'sell'.
From Low German 'betalen', a Hanseatic loan. Regular: betaler, betalte, har betalt. 'Å betale med kort' = to pay by card.
Neuter: 'kortet'. 'Bankkort' is the debit card used for nearly everything; Norway is close to cashless. Also a postcard or playing card.
Plural only; definite 'kontantene'. From Italian 'contante' via German. Many cafés and buses no longer accept cash.
Definite 'krona' or 'kronen', plural 'kroner', abbreviated 'kr' or NOK. Literally 'crown', like the Swedish and Danish currencies. 100 øre = 1 krone.
Definite 'kvitteringa' or 'kvitteringen'. From the verb 'å kvittere' (to sign for), ultimately Latin 'quietus' (free of debt), the same root as English 'quit'.
Definite 'posen'. A shopping bag, charged for at the till. A handbag or rucksack is 'veske' or 'sekk'. 'Pose' is pronounced 'POO-seh'.
'Kjøpe' (buy) + 'senter' (centre). Neuter: 'kjøpesenteret'. 'Senter' is spelled with an 's'.
'Til' (to) + 'bud' (bid, offer). Neuter: 'tilbudet'. 'På tilbud' = on offer. 'Salg' is a sale (reduced prices).

example.target: Laksen er på tilbud i dag.

note: Definite 'kassa' or 'kassen'. Originally a box or crate (like English 'case'), hence the cash box. 'Selvbetjent kasse' = self-service checkout.
Regular verb. 'Å handle mat' = to buy groceries. Also 'to act' (handle = action). Related to 'hand', like English 'handle'.

example.target: Jeg må handle mat til middag.
example.en: I have to buy food for dinner.

note: Definite 'gaven'. From 'å gi' (to give), like English 'gift'. Note the false friend: Norwegian 'gift' means 'married' or 'poison'.
Invariable. From Latin 'gratis'. 'Fri' means free as in liberty, not free of charge.
Neuter form of 'åpen', used on signs and with 'det': 'Det er åpent'. 'Åpningstider' = opening hours.

example.en: Is the shop open on Sunday?

note: Past participle of 'å stenge' (to close, shut). 'Stengt' on a door sign; 'lukket' is used for a closed object or a private event.
Neuter: 'paret'. 'Et par sko' = a pair of shoes; 'et par dager' = a couple of days; also 'a couple' (people). Same as English 'pair/par'.
Definite 'banken'. 'Minibank' is a cash machine. Bank ID (BankID) is the login used for nearly all public services.
'Lomme' (pocket) + 'bok' (book). Definite 'lommeboka'. Plural 'lommebøker'.
The 'd' is silent: 'glaa'. Neuter 'glad', plural 'glade'. 'Glad i' = fond of: 'Jeg er glad i deg' is the everyday 'I love you' for family and friends.

example.en: I love you (I am fond of you).

note: Neuter 'trist', plural 'triste'. From French 'triste'. 'Lei seg' is the more colloquial way to say someone is sad or upset.
Neuter 'sint', plural 'sinte'. 'Sint på' = angry with someone. Related to 'sinn' (mind, temper).

example.target: Hvorfor er du sint på meg?
example.en: Why are you angry with me?

note: Neuter 'redd', plural 'redde'. 'Redd for' = afraid of. Cognate with Old Norse 'hræddr'; the 'h' was lost.
Neuter 'trøtt', plural 'trøtte'. Also spelled 'trett'. 'Trøtt av' = tired of (fed up). 'Sliten' is tired in the sense of worn out.

example.target: Jeg er så trøtt i dag.

note: Neuter 'sultent', plural 'sultne'. From 'sult' (hunger). 'Jeg er sulten' is the normal way; there is no 'I have hunger'.
Neuter 'tørst', plural 'tørste'. From 'tørr' (dry); compare English 'thirst'. 'Jeg er tørst' = I am thirsty.
From 'lykke' (happiness, luck), a Low German loan. Stronger and more lasting than 'glad'. Final 'g' silent: 'LUK-keh-li'.
Definite 'følelsen', plural 'følelser'. From 'å føle' (to feel) + '-else'. 'Jeg har en følelse av at ...' = I have a feeling that ...
Definite 'kjærligheten'. From 'kjær' (dear) + '-lig' + '-het' (like English '-ness'). Pronounced 'HYÆR-li-het' with the soft 'kj'.
Regular verb. Strong and romantic; between family and friends Norwegians usually say 'glad i' instead. 'Jeg elsker deg' = I love you.
Regular: liker, likte, har likt. Pronounced 'LEE-keh'. 'Jeg liker ikke fisk' = I don't like fish. Cognate with English 'like'.
Regular: hater, hatet, har hatet. Pronounced 'HAA-teh'. The noun is 'hat'. Cognate with English 'hate'.
Regular verb. For missing people or things you lack: 'Jeg savner deg'. Missing a bus is 'å miste bussen'. Nynorsk: 'sakne'.
Reflexive: 'Jeg gleder meg til jul' = I am looking forward to Christmas. Without 'til', 'å glede seg' is simply to be glad or to rejoice.

example.en: I am looking forward to the weekend!

note: 'Å være lei seg' = to be sad/upset: 'Hun er lei seg'. Change the reflexive: 'jeg er lei meg'. 'Lei av' means fed up with: 'Jeg er lei av regn'.

example.target: Jeg er lei meg for det.

note: Past participle of 'å bekymre' (to worry), a Low German loan. 'Bekymret for' = worried about. The noun is 'en bekymring'.
Neuter 'nervøst', plural 'nervøse'. Stress on the last syllable, as in French 'nerveux'. 'Nervøs for' = nervous about.
Neuter 'stolt', plural 'stolte'. 'Stolt av' = proud of. From Low German 'stolt', the same word as German 'stolz'.
Participle of 'å overraske', from German 'überraschen'. 'En overraskelse' = a surprise. The 'over' means 'over', the 'rask' part means 'quick'.
Reflexive: 'Jeg kjeder meg' = I'm bored. Without 'seg', 'å kjede' is to bore someone. 'Kjedelig' = boring. Soft 'kj': 'HYEH-deh'.

example.en: The children are bored in the car.

note: Neuter 'flaut', plural 'flaue'. 'Det var flaut' = that was embarrassing. From Low German 'flau' (weak, faint). Also describes a weak wind: 'flau bris'.
Neuter 'rolig', plural 'rolige'. From 'ro' (calm, rest). 'Ta det med ro' = take it easy. Final 'g' silent: 'ROO-li'.
Strong verb: ler, lo, har ledd. 'Å le av' = to laugh at. Cognate with English 'laugh'; the final consonant was lost in Norwegian.
Strong verb: gråter, gråt, har grått. From Old Norse 'gráta'; English 'greet' in Scots still means 'to weep'.
Irregular: har, hadde, har hatt. Also the auxiliary for the perfect: 'Jeg har spist' = I have eaten. Same form for all persons.
Irregular: gjør, gjorde, har gjort. The 'g' is silent: 'YUR-eh', 'yur', 'YOOR-deh', 'yort'. 'Hva gjør du?' = what are you doing?

example.en: What are you doing at the weekend?

note: Strong: går, gikk, har gått. Means walk, not travel: 'Jeg går til jobb' = I walk to work. For going by vehicle use 'dra' or 'reise'. 'Det går bra' = it's going well.

example.en: We walked home after the party.

note: Strong: kommer, kom, har kommet. 'Kom inn!' = come in. 'Å komme fra' = to come from: 'Hvor kommer du fra?'
Strong: ser, så, har sett. 'Se på' = to look at/watch: 'se på TV'. 'Vi ses' (we'll see each other) uses the reciprocal -s form.
Irregular: sier, sa, har sagt. The 'g' in 'sagt' is silent. 'Hva sa du?' = what did you say? 'Si det!' = tell me / go on!
Regular verb from Low German 'snacken' (to chat), a Hanseatic loan that replaced the older 'tale'. 'Snakker du engelsk?' = do you speak English?
Strong: sover, sov, har sovet. 'Sov godt!' = sleep well. 'Å sovne' is the separate verb for falling asleep.
Regular: våkner, våknet, har våknet. Intransitive (you wake up). To wake someone else is 'å vekke'. Cognate with English 'waken'.
'Stå' (stand) + 'opp' (up): getting out of bed. Standing up from a chair is 'å reise seg'. Past 'sto opp' (also 'stod').
Strong: tar, tok, har tatt. English 'take' is itself a loan from Old Norse 'taka'. Used for transport ('ta bussen') and 'ta det med ro'.
Strong: gir, ga (or gav), har gitt. Pronounced 'yee'. 'Gi meg ...' = give me ... 'Gi opp' = give up.
Strong: får, fikk, har fått. Extremely common: 'Kan jeg få ...' (can I have), 'få lov' (be allowed), 'få se' (get to see). Cognate with Old English 'fon' (to seize).

example.target: Jeg fikk en gave av mora mi.
example.en: I got a present from my mother.

note: 'Å lage mat' (to make food) is the usual verb for cooking. Regular: lager, laget (or lagde), har laget. 'Lag' is also a team.
Strong: hjelper, hjalp, har hjulpet. Silent 'h': 'YEL-peh'. 'Kan du hjelpe meg?' = can you help me? 'Hjelp!' = help!
Regular: tenker, tenkte, har tenkt. 'Tenke på' = think about. The noun 'tanken' (the thought) is a classic pitch-accent pair with 'tanken' (the tank): same letters, different melody.
Irregular: vet, visste, har visst. Only for facts; knowing a person or place is 'å kjenne'. 'Jeg vet ikke' = I don't know. Cognate with English 'wit'.
Modal: kan, kunne, har kunnet. Followed by a bare infinitive without 'å': 'Jeg kan svømme'. Also 'to know (a language or skill)': 'Jeg kan norsk'.

example.en: Can you speak a little more slowly?

note: Modal: vil, ville, har villet. 'Vil' means 'want to', not future 'will': 'Jeg vil ha kaffe' = I want coffee. The future uses 'skal' or 'kommer til å'.

example.target: Vil du ha noe å drikke?
example.en: Do you want something to drink?

note: Modal: må, måtte, har måttet. 'Jeg må gå' = I have to go. 'Må ikke' means 'must not' (forbidden); 'need not' is 'trenger ikke'.
Strong: blir, ble, har blitt. Both 'become' ('bli syk' = get ill) and 'remain' ('bli hjemme' = stay home). Also forms the passive: 'bli sett' = be seen.

example.en: It is going to get cold tonight.

note: From Low German 'beginnen'. Regular: begynner, begynte, har begynt. 'Begynne på' = start on; 'begynne med' = start with. Stress on '-gyn-'.
Regular: venter, ventet, har ventet. 'Vente på' = wait for. Also 'to expect': 'å vente barn' = to be expecting a baby.
Regular: hører, hørte, har hørt. 'Høre på' = listen to (music). 'Vi høres' = we'll be in touch (literally 'we'll hear each other').
Regular: trenger, trengte, har trengt. 'Jeg trenger hjelp' = I need help. 'Trenger ikke' = needn't; the modal 'behøve' is a formal alternative.
Silent 'h': 'vaa'. Most question words start with a silent 'hv-', a spelling kept from Old Norse 'hv-'. Nynorsk uses 'kva'.
Silent 'h': 'vem'. Used for both 'who' and 'whom'. 'Hvem er det?' = who is it?
Silent 'h': 'voor'. Also 'how' before an adjective: 'hvor gammel' (how old), 'hvor mye' (how much), 'hvor lenge' (how long).
Pronounced 'nawr'. Both the question 'when?' and the conjunction 'when(ever)' for present or future; for a single past event use 'da'.
'Hvor' + 'for', like old English 'wherefore'. Answer with 'fordi' (because). Silent 'h'.
Silent 'h': 'VOR-dan'. 'Hvordan har du det?' = how are you? Nynorsk: 'korleis'. Note 'hvor' alone before adjectives: 'hvor mye'.
Agrees with the noun: 'hvilken bil' (m/f), 'hvilket hus' (neuter), 'hvilke biler' (plural). Silent 'h'.
The 'g' is silent: 'aw', so it sounds just like 'å' (to), a classic spelling trap even for Norwegians ('og/å-feil').
Pronounced 'menn'. Beware: 'menn' with double 'n' is 'men' (plural of 'mann').
'Enten ... eller' = either ... or. Also softens a question at the end: 'Kommer du, eller?' = are you coming, or what?
Goes after the verb in main clauses: 'Jeg vet ikke'. Nynorsk uses 'ikkje', which you will also hear in western dialects.
'Og' + 'så'. Pronounced 'OS-so' with the 'g' silent. 'Jeg også' = me too.
Pronounced 'BAA-reh'. Very common softener: 'bare bra' (just fine), 'bare hyggelig' (my pleasure), 'bare vent' (just wait).
From 'velde' (power, might), so originally 'mighty'. Final 'g' silent: 'VEL-di'. 'Kjempe-' as a prefix is the colloquial 'super-': 'kjempebra'.
Pronounced 'yai'; the 'g' is silent. Object form 'meg' ('may'), possessive 'min/mi/mitt'. Nynorsk: 'eg', and many dialects say 'e' or 'æ'.
Object form 'deg' ('day'). Norway dropped the polite 'De' in the 1970s; 'du' is now used with everyone, including the prime minister.
Object form 'ham' (or 'han'; both are accepted). 'Hans' = his. For things, use 'den' (m/f) or 'det' (neuter) rather than han/hun.
Object form 'henne', possessive 'hennes'. Pronounced 'hoon'. 'Hen' is a newer gender-neutral pronoun, borrowed from Swedish, used by some speakers.
Object form 'oss', possessive 'vår/vårt/våre'. Pronounced 'vee'.
Pronounced 'dee', object form 'dem'. English 'they/them' were borrowed from Old Norse 'þeir/þeim'; Norwegian 'de/dem' descend from the same words. 'De' is also 'the' in the plural: 'de nye bilene'.
The 't' is silent: 'deh'. The neuter 'it', the dummy subject ('Det regner'), and 'that' before a neuter noun ('det huset'). 'Den' is the m/f equivalent.
From 'kan' + 'skje' (can happen), like English 'maybe' is 'may be'. Pronounced 'KAN-sheh'. Usually first in the sentence: 'Kanskje det'.

example.target: Kanskje vi kan møtes i morgen?

note: Pronounced 'OF-teh'. 'Hvor ofte?' = how often? Cognate with English 'oft/often'.
'All' + 'tid' (time). The 'd' is silent: 'AL-ti'. Goes after the verb: 'Jeg drikker alltid kaffe'.
Pronounced 'AL-dri'. Like 'ikke', it follows the verb in main clauses: 'Jeg har aldri vært i Tromsø'. From Old Norse 'aldrigi' (not in a lifetime).

example.target: Jeg har aldri vært i Tromsø.
example.en: I have never been to Tromsø.

note: Neuter 'stort', plural 'store'. Comparative 'større', superlative 'størst'. 'Storting' (great assembly) is the parliament. Cognate with Old Norse 'stórr'.
Highly irregular: 'liten' (m), 'lita' (f), 'lite' (n), 'små' (plural), definite 'lille'. Comparative 'mindre', superlative 'minst'.

example.target: Vi har et lite hus og to små barn.
example.en: We have a small house and two small children.

note: Neuter 'godt', plural 'gode'; comparative 'bedre', superlative 'best', like English. Silent 'd': 'goo'. 'Godt' also means 'tasty' and 'sweets' (lørdagsgodt).
Neuter 'dårlig', plural 'dårlige'. Final 'g' silent: 'DAWR-li'. Comparative 'verre', superlative 'verst'. 'Dårlig' also means 'unwell'.
Neuter 'nytt', plural 'nye'. Rounded 'y' vowel. 'Nyheter' = the news; 'nytt år' = new year. Cognate with English 'new'.
Neuter 'gammelt', plural 'gamle'. Comparative 'eldre', superlative 'eldst' (from a different root, like old/elder). 'Gamlebyen' = the old town.
Neuter 'ungt', plural 'unge'. Comparative 'yngre', superlative 'yngst'. 'Ungdom' = youth; 'en unge' = a kid.
Neuter 'langt', plural 'lange'. Comparative 'lengre', superlative 'lengst'. 'Lenge' is the adverb for time: 'Hvor lenge?' (how long?).
Neuter 'kort', plural 'korte'. Same spelling as 'et kort' (a card). From Latin 'curtus' via Low German, the source of English 'curt'.
Neuter 'høyt', plural 'høye'. Covers tall people, high mountains and loud sounds ('snakk høyere' = speak louder). Pronounced 'huh-ee'.
Neuter 'lavt', plural 'lave'. Also 'quiet' of sounds and 'short' of people (never 'kort' for a person). 'Lavpris' = low-price.
Neuter 'fint', plural 'fine'. The all-purpose positive word: 'fint vær', 'en fin dag', 'Det er fint' (that's fine). From French 'fin' via Low German.
Neuter 'pent', plural 'pene'. Also 'neat/proper': 'pent vær' (fair weather), 'oppføre seg pent' (behave nicely). 'Vakker' is 'beautiful'.
Neuter 'stygt', plural 'stygge'. Also 'nasty': 'stygt vær' (foul weather), 'stygge ord' (bad language).
Neuter 'raskt', plural 'raske'. The adverb 'fort' (quickly) is more common in speech: 'Kjør fort!' Cognate with English 'rash'.
Neuter 'langsomt', plural 'langsomme'. In speech 'sakte' (slowly) or 'treg' (sluggish) are more common. 'Snakk saktere' = speak more slowly.
Neuter 'lett', plural 'lette'. Both 'easy' and 'light in weight', like German 'leicht'. 'Lettmelk' = semi-skimmed milk.

example.target: Norsk er ikke så vanskelig, det er ganske lett.
example.en: Norwegian is not so difficult, it is quite easy.

note: Neuter 'tungt', plural 'tunge'. Also 'hard' emotionally: 'en tung dag'. 'Tungt' before a verb means 'with difficulty'. Not related to 'tunge' (tongue).
Neuter 'vanskelig', plural 'vanskelige'. Final 'g' silent: 'VAN-skeh-li'. From 'vanske' (difficulty). 'Vanskelig å si' = hard to say.
Neuter 'enkelt', plural 'enkle'. Also 'single': 'enkeltbillett' (single ticket), 'enkeltrom' (single room). 'Enkelt' can mean 'simply'.
Neuter 'rent', plural 'rene'. Also 'pure': 'rent vann'. 'Renhold' = cleaning (as a service). Cognate with German 'rein'.
Neuter 'skittent', plural 'skitne'. From 'skitt' (dirt), which is also a mild swear word and appears in the good-luck wish to anglers, 'skitt fiske'.
Neuter 'viktig', plural 'viktige'. From Low German 'wichtich', literally 'weighty' (German 'wichtig'). Final 'g' silent: 'VIK-ti'.

example.target: Det er viktig å lære norsk.
example.en: It is important to learn Norwegian.

note: Neuter 'morsomt', plural 'morsomme'. Both 'amusing' and 'enjoyable': 'en morsom film', 'Det var morsomt!' From 'moro' (fun).
Neuter 'kjedelig', plural 'kjedelige'. From 'å kjede' (to bore). Also 'a pity, annoying': 'Så kjedelig!' = what a shame. Soft 'kj' and silent 'g'.
Definite 'byen', plural 'byer'. From Old Norse 'býr' (farm, settlement); the '-by' in English place names like Whitby and Derby is the same word. 'I byen' = in town.

example.target: Skal vi dra inn til byen?

note: Neuter, a Latin loan; plural 'sentre' or 'sentra'. Spelled with 's'. 'Oslo sentrum' is the city centre; road signs just say 'Sentrum'.
Neuter: 'torget'. From Old Norse 'torg', itself a loan from Old Russian 'torg' (market) via trade. 'Fisketorget' in Bergen is the famous fish market.
Definite 'parken'. Frognerparken in Oslo holds Vigeland's sculptures. 'Nasjonalpark' = national park, of which Norway has over forty.
Definite 'kirka' or 'kirken'. From Greek 'kyriakon' (the Lord's house), like English 'church' and Scots 'kirk'. Nynorsk: 'kyrkje'. 'Stavkirke' = stave church.
Neuter: 'biblioteket'. Stress on the last syllable. Libraries are free and open to all; Oslo's Deichman is the main one.
Neuter: 'museet' (the -um drops), plural 'museer'. Oslo's museum island Bygdøy has the Viking ships and the Fram polar ship.

example.en: The museum is closed on Mondays.

note: Definite 'kinoen'. Short for 'kinematograf', as in German 'Kino'. 'Å gå på kino' = to go to the cinema. Films are subtitled, not dubbed.

example.target: Skal vi gå på kino i kveld?
example.en: Shall we go to the cinema tonight?

note: Neuter: 'teateret' or 'teatret'. Spelled without 'h'. Nationaltheatret in Oslo is also the name of a central station.
Definite 'bygningen'. From 'å bygge' (to build). 'Et bygg' is the shorter everyday word for a building.
'Råd' (council, advice) + 'hus'. Oslo Rådhus, with its two brick towers, hosts the Nobel Peace Prize ceremony every December.
'Politi' + 'stasjon'. The police are 'politiet'; the emergency number is 112. Norwegian police are normally unarmed.
Definite 'kiosken'. Narvesen and 7-Eleven kiosks sell hot dogs, newspapers and bus tickets. The word came via Turkish 'köşk' (pavilion).
'Land' + 's' + 'by'. Norway has few true villages; people more often say 'bygd' (rural community) or 'tettsted' (built-up area).
'By' + 'del' (part). Oslo has fifteen 'bydeler', such as Grünerløkka and Frogner.
Definite 'kommunen'. The local council that runs schools, kindergartens and care. 'Kommunen' is a word you will hear constantly in daily life.
Neuter: 'landet', plural 'land'. The 'd' is silent: 'lann'. 'På landet' = in the countryside. Norway is 'Norge' (Nynorsk 'Noreg').
'Hoved' (head, main) + 'stad' (city, an older word for 'by', seen in Stavanger and Kristiansand). Silent 'd' in both parts.
Definite 'havna'. From Old Norse 'hǫfn'; English 'haven' is the same word. Bergen's 'Bryggen', the old Hanseatic wharf, is a UNESCO site.
'Trening' (training) + 's' + 'senter'. 'Å trene' = to work out. Norwegians also say 'å gå på trening'.
'Barne' (children) + 'hage' (garden), a calque of German 'Kindergarten'. Nearly all children from age one attend; 'å levere i barnehagen' = to drop off at nursery.

example.target: Jeg henter barna i barnehagen klokka fire.
example.en: I pick the children up from nursery at four.

note: 'Leke' (to play) + 'plass'. 'Å leke' is children's play; playing an instrument or sport is 'å spille'.
Neuter: 'bakeriet'. From 'å bake' + '-eri' (a place of business, like '-ery'). Stress on the final '-i'.
Definite 'frisøren'. From French 'friseur' (one who curls). 'Å klippe seg' = to get a haircut (literally 'to cut oneself').
'Bensin' + 'stasjon'. Open late, and in small places it doubles as café, kiosk and social hub; the hot dogs are a national institution.
